noteBlocks.lede: Your body fights microorganisms in three ways: it keeps them out, it engulfs the ones that get in, and it makes antibodies that fit one kind exactly. It also remembers, which is why the same illness rarely strikes twice. Nearly every mark here is a precise word.

Explain the faster second response with memory lymphocytes, and tell active from passive immunity.

noteBlocks.md: Every day microorganisms land on your skin, and almost none make you ill. Your body stops most at the door, destroys those that get in, and remembers the ones it has met.

noteBlocks.md: The first line is **barriers**. The **skin** is a barrier microorganisms cannot cross; **mucous membranes** in the nose and airways trap them in sticky mucus; **blood clotting** seals a cut.

noteBlocks.md:
How a cut is sealed:
1. **Platelets** at the cut turn fibrinogen, a plasma protein, into insoluble **fibrin** threads.
2. The threads form a mesh that traps red blood cells: a **clot**, which dries to a **scab**.
3. The clot stops blood loss and keeps microorganisms out.

noteBlocks.prompt: When the skin is cut, platelets turn fibrinogen into threads of ______, which form a mesh that traps blood cells.
noteBlocks.answer: fibrin | fibrin threads | insoluble fibrin | fibrins | fibrin fibres
noteBlocks.explain: Clotting starts with the platelets. They turn fibrinogen, which is dissolved in the plasma, into fibrin, which is not: its threads make the mesh that traps the red blood cells and becomes the clot. The threads are fibrin.

noteBlocks.md: Microorganisms carry molecules on their surface called **antigens**, and each kind has its own shape. White blood cells called **lymphocytes** respond by making **antibodies** whose shape is **complementary** to that antigen: the reverse of it, so the two fit together like a key in its lock.

noteBlocks.title: Why one antibody fits one microorganism
noteBlocks.md: A complementary shape fits one antigen only. So the antibodies made against one microorganism attach to that kind and no other, and a new microorganism needs new antibodies. The shapes are never the same: the same shape could not fit over it.

noteBlocks.prompt: How does the shape of an antibody compare with the shape of the antigen it attaches to?
options: it is complementary to the antigen
it is the same shape as the antigen
noteBlocks.answer: it is complementary to the antigen
noteBlocks.explain: Look at the figure again: the antibody's tip is a socket the antigen's point slides into, the reverse of the antigen, not a copy of it. And it fits the antigen on the surface, not the whole microorganism. The word the marks need is complementary.

noteBlocks.md: An antibody has more than one tip, so it can attach to two microorganisms at once. Thousands of antibodies do this and **clump** the microorganisms together. Stuck in a clump, they cannot move, spread or reproduce, so there are fewer of them to cause symptoms.

What happens next, in the marks' own words:
1. A different white blood cell, a **phagocyte**, moves to the clump.
2. It **engulfs** the clump, surrounding it.
3. It **digests** the microorganisms inside it.

noteBlocks.title: Three words, three marks
noteBlocks.md: The Summer 2024 report asked candidates to use the ordinary words for this step. Name the phagocyte, say it engulfs, say it digests. 'The white blood cells eat them' names none of the three.

noteBlocks.prompt: After antibodies clump microorganisms together, a phagocyte engulfs the clump and then ______ it.
noteBlocks.answer: digests | digest | digested | breaks down | break down | breaks it down | digests it | digest it | breaks them down | digests them | digesting
noteBlocks.explain: A phagocyte deals with a clump in two steps: first it engulfs it, wrapping itself round the clump, then it digests the microorganisms inside. The second step is the one asked for: it digests it.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Biology Revision "The Immune System"
noteBlocks.why: A short lesson on phagocytes, lymphocytes and antibodies, made for another exam board. Watch for the three words: engulf, digest, complementary.

noteBlocks.title: What the video adds, and what it leaves out
noteBlocks.md: Lessons for other boards add antitoxins, a third job for white blood cells that CCEA does not examine. They usually leave out active and passive immunity, which CCEA does ask for: learn those from this note.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which white blood cells make antibodies?
noteBlocks.explain: There are two jobs and two kinds of white blood cell. Lymphocytes make antibodies against a particular antigen; phagocytes engulf and digest. Platelets are not white blood cells at all: they clot the blood. So antibodies come from lymphocytes.

noteBlocks.alt: A graph of antibody concentration against time. After the first exposure, on day 0, antibodies appear on day 6 and rise slowly to a small peak of 20 units on day 14. After a second exposure to the same antigen, on day 35, antibodies appear on day 37 and rise fast to a peak of 120 units on day 42.
noteBlocks.caption: After the second exposure to the same antigen, antibodies appear sooner and reach a far higher level.

noteBlocks.md: The first time a microorganism gets in, making the right antibodies takes days, and you may feel ill meanwhile. Some of the lymphocytes then stay in the blood as **memory lymphocytes**. If the same microorganism returns, they recognise its antigen at once.

Read the graph:
1. First exposure: antibodies appear after 6 days and peak at 20 units.
2. Second exposure: they appear after 2 days and peak at 120 units.
3. 120 ÷ 20 = 6: the second response is faster, 6 times larger, and lasts longer.

noteBlocks.prompt: On another person's antibody graph, the first peak is 15 units and the peak after a second exposure to the same antigen is 75 units. How many times greater is the second peak?
noteBlocks.explain: "How many times greater" asks for a division, not a subtraction: the larger peak divided by the smaller, as with 120 ÷ 20 on the graph above. Here 75 ÷ 15 = 5 times greater.

noteBlocks.md: Ask one question: did your own lymphocytes make the antibodies? If yes, after an infection or a vaccine, it is **active immunity**, and it lasts because memory lymphocytes remain. If the antibodies arrived ready-made, from a mother's milk or an injection, it is **passive immunity**.

Passive immunity works at once but fades. In the figure, antibodies are injected on day 0 at 96 units. They are broken down and never replaced, so the level falls below the 24 units needed on day 16: immune from day 0 to day 16.

noteBlocks.prompt: A newborn baby gets antibodies from its mother's milk. What type of immunity is this?
noteBlocks.explain: The deciding question is who made the antibodies. The baby's own lymphocytes did not: they arrived ready-made in the milk. Ready-made antibodies give passive immunity, which protects straight away but fades because no memory lymphocytes are made.

noteBlocks.md: **Choose the antibody** (2023). Look for the socket the antigen would slot into. A: tips the same shape as the antigen, so no. B: a triangular socket, the reverse of the triangular antigen, so yes. C: a square socket, so no. Answer: B, because its shape is complementary to the antigen.

parts.stem:
Describe how blood clots when the skin is cut, and explain how clotting helps to defend the body.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; the ideas are ordered very clearly and follow on from one another; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; the ideas are ordered reasonably well and mostly follow on; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.

indicativeContent.point: platelets at the cut start the clotting
platelets turn fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads
the mesh traps red blood cells
a clot forms, which dries into a scab
the clot seals the wound, so microorganisms cannot enter

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Seven creditworthy points in two halves, as CCEA sets this question: the process (platelets; insoluble fibrin; a mesh; trapping blood cells; a clot or scab) and the defence (stopping blood loss; keeping microorganisms out). An answer that describes the clot but never says what it keeps out has not answered the second half and should not reach the top band.

hints: Describe first: platelets, fibrin, mesh, trapped cells, clot, scab.
Then explain: what does the clot stop, and what does it keep out?
parts.workedSolution: When the skin is cut, platelets in the blood start the clotting process: they convert fibrinogen, a protein in the plasma, into insoluble fibrin threads, which form a mesh across the wound. The mesh traps red blood cells, and a clot forms, which dries to a scab. The clot stops blood loss, and it seals the cut so that microorganisms cannot enter the body.

prompts.prompt: Name the three barriers that keep microorganisms out of the body.
prompts.answer: Skin, mucous membranes and blood clotting.

prompts.prompt: What do lymphocytes make, and in response to what?
prompts.answer: Antibodies, in response to antigens on a microorganism.

prompts.prompt: How does an antibody's shape compare with its antigen's?
prompts.answer: It is complementary: the reverse of the antigen's shape, so it fits that antigen only.

prompts.prompt: How does clumping help to defend the body?
prompts.answer: Clumped microorganisms cannot move, spread or reproduce, and phagocytes can engulf them.

prompts.prompt: Why is the second response to the same microorganism faster and larger?
prompts.answer: Memory lymphocytes from the first infection recognise it and make antibodies faster and in greater numbers.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between active and passive immunity?
prompts.answer: Active: your own lymphocytes make the antibodies. Passive: antibodies arrive ready-made and soon disappear.
They engulf microorganisms and digest them.

findings.asked: Identify the antibody, describe how it matches the antigen, explain immobilisation, then describe phagocytosis.
findings.wentWrong: Identifying it was easy; describing the match was not - 'the same shape' instead of complementary, and fitting 'the microorganism' rather than its antigen. Immobilisation answers were vague, and phagocytosis descriptions wandered instead of using the three expected words.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Said the antibody's shape is complementary to the antigen, that clumping stops the microorganisms reproducing or spreading, and that phagocytes engulf and digest the clump.
findings.rule: Complementary, not the same; antigen, not microorganism; phagocyte, engulf, digest.

findings.asked: The same antibody question at Foundation.
findings.wentWrong: Same pattern: the complementary idea was the sticking point and phagocytosis lacked the standard vocabulary.
findings.rule: Use the textbook words; they are the mark scheme.

findings.asked: Choose which antibody would be produced against a drawn microorganism.
findings.wentWrong: Many did not choose the antibody whose shape was complementary to the drawn antigen, though most still scored well on the rest of the question.
findings.rule: Match the antibody to the antigen's shape like a lock and key.

insight.ruleToRemember: Antigens are on the surface of the microorganism; lymphocytes make antibodies whose shape is complementary to that antigen; the antibodies bind and clump (immobilise) the microorganisms, which phagocytes then engulf and digest.
insight.aStarSignal: Choosing the right antibody from shapes and then explaining the whole sequence in the scheme's own vocabulary.
